## v5.1.0 — mentions, thread unreads, and labels on every message

20 tools. The catch-up can finally see what it exists for, and every message now says who wrote it.

### The flagship was blind

`slack_conversations_unreads` filtered on `unread_count_display` alone. Measured against a real workspace before this release, it returned **zero** conversations while ten mentions were outstanding — every one in a channel whose unread count was zero because the channel had been opened.

It now also calls `client.counts`, the endpoint Slack's own web client uses for its sidebar badges. Same workspace after: 7 conversations, 10 mentions, and one conversation the listing page never reached. Mentions sort above unread volume.

`client.counts` is undocumented, so every read of it is guarded and the response names which endpoint answered. When it fails, the tool degrades to exactly the previous view and says what is missing from it.

### Every message says who wrote it

Slack is a shared bus — Slack Connect participants, guests, apps relaying content from outside Slack entirely — and the same toolset that reads also writes. Every message now carries `origin` (`self`, `internal`, `external`, `bot`, `unknown`) and `author_trusted`, from fields Slack already returns, at no extra API call.

Building the receipt for it found something worse. Slack omits `team` from messages written inside your own workspace, so the classifier matched almost nothing: 11 of 20 messages on a real channel came back `unknown`, every one of them a colleague. A conversation Slack reports as not shared cannot hold an outside author, so a team-less author there is internal. Same channel after: unknown 11 → 0.

### What you get

- **`client.counts` merged into unreads** — per-conversation mention counts, unread thread replies, and the conversations a single listing page cannot reach.
- **`slack_session_report`** — messages read, how many were outside-authored and by which origin, writes attempted, writes held. Counts only; no message text, channel name or user id.
- **`--read-only` / `SLACK_MCP_READ_ONLY=1`** — the write tools are withheld from `tools/list` *and* refused at dispatch. An absent tool needs no trust.
- **`continuity` on `slack_catch_me_up`** — commitments, owner gaps, open questions, each row carrying the text that matched and a permalink to the message. The rules are shallow and the output says so.
- **A published injection corpus** (`docs/INJECTION-CORPUS.md`) — bidi overrides, zero-width splits, tool-call mimicry, bot relays, attacker-settable identity fields, so other MCP authors can test their own servers.
- **CodeQL and OSV-Scanner** over the code and the dependency tree.
- **`--doctor --security`** — six checks, each with a one-line remedy. No score.

### Fixed

- The strict send hold could be switched off by the call it was meant to restrain, and `slack_catch_me_up` never armed it at all.
- The setup wizard advertised an extraction path the code does not run, and every failure repeated one fixed instruction regardless of the reason code beside it. Setup now prints the client configuration instead of linking to a page describing it.
- Commands an `npx` user cannot run were removed from the docs and the bug-report template.
- Identity-keyed caches are cleared on a token refresh; a refresh can land on a different workspace.

### The README moves again

The hero is a split screen: you ask for a jammed printer's admin PIN on one side, and on the other the #facilities channel lights up the message that had it all along — posted in October, zero reactions. Three people asked. Nobody searched. It is a GIF, so GitHub plays it inline, and it re-records byte-for-byte from source.

### Honest about the limits

A provenance label is advice to the calling model: unsigned, strippable downstream. The `strict` hold is released by a flag the caller sets, so it records a send without proving a human approved it. Display names and channel topics still reach the model unlabelled. `--read-only` is the only guarantee that does not depend on the model. All of it is written down in [SECURITY.md](../SECURITY.md).

The README used to say session credentials rotate every one or two weeks. On one real workspace a credential written on 2026-07-04 still authenticated 94 days later. That is one credential, not a distribution — but it is measured, and it is now stated that way.

### Compatibility

Default behaviour adds keys and removes none. `SLACK_MCP_PROVENANCE=off` restores the previous output shape. The `provenance` argument on a read may tighten labelling and no longer loosen it.

### Install

```bash
npx -y @jtalk22/slack-mcp --setup
```
